title: Palestinians and US journalist injured by Israeli settlers in West Bank harvest attack
content: Dozens of masked settlers have attacked Palestinians and set fire to cars and olive trees during the annual olive harvest in the occupied West Bank. A BBC team witnessed one of several attacks in farmland near the Palestinian village of Abu Falah. A local official said the attacks had injured 12 Palestinians, including four dual Palestinian American citizens. A foreign journalist was also among those hurt. Driving into the area early in the morning, we came across the first signs of the violence : a stream of cars carrying wounded Palestinian olive farmers racing out along the narrow stony track, piled high with olive picking equipment, as smoke rose from several fires nearby. The bloodied face of Majdi Fheed peered out from the backseat of one car. "We were getting our olive trees and almost 15 Jewish guys … started attacking us with guns, with rocks, with special weapons. They hit me on my head [and] my neck – look, I am bleeding!" Yaser AlKam, a council member from the neighbouring village of Turmus Aya told me Majdi - an American citizen - was attacked by settlers with nail-studded sticks, and needed treatment for deep wounds on his head. His elderly mother was also injured. Another man ferrying the injured to hospital told us that settlers had attacked them with sticks while they harvested their olives, and had burned three cars – including one of his own. "As soon as we got to the land and put our things on the ground, they started to come, so we ran away" said a woman next to him. Asked about the violence, a US State Department spokesperson said they were aware of the reports. "We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and call for investigations, arrests, and convictions, of those responsible," the spokesperson said. Watching the vehicles stream past her, 73-year-old Imm Khaldoun told me emphatically that, no matter what happened, she would always return to her land. "This is my land. It's my right [to be here]" she told me. The UN says the past two weeks have already seen more attacks by violent Israeli settlers than during the entire harvest season last year. Olive picking in the West Bank is now a test of speed, with trees rapidly stripped of fruit as soon as the sun rises, before violent Israeli settlers attack. In another olive orchard nearby, we watched as dozens of farmers used power-tools to strip the trees as fast as they could – one eye on the ridge above us, where a group of settlers at a new illegal outpost had already gathered, and were watching the olive harvest below. Standing on ladders, the Palestinian farmers worked quickly, sending streams of olives onto the plastic sheets laid out under the trees. Three villages had come together to harvest these olives, the landowner Amin Khalil, told me, as a form of protection against attack. He said his land was now surrounded by seven Jewish settlements and outposts. All Israeli settlements are illegal under international law. Outposts – small encampments on hilltops – are illegal under Israeli law as well, but many still receive state support. "This is a hotspot – there are seven settlements around here," Amin Khalil told me. "This year, all the people came together because when there are just a few people working alone at the edge of the village, the settlers attack. So all the families are working together today." But the tactic doesn't work today. As we watch, dozens of settlers, all dressed in black, begin moving down the hill towards us, setting fire to several groups of olive trees. There are shouts of panic from the Palestinian farmers, yelling for children to get out of the field. Some begin swiftly wrapping up the olives to leave. But with large numbers of people on both sides, the confrontation stalls into an uneasy stalemate. We see settlers with slingshots hurl stones towards us, and young Palestinian men running to throw stones in return. As Israeli forces arrive, the standoff explodes into action. Settlers begin running down towards us as the farmers swiftly retreat. Some Palestinians set off fireworks to try and push the settlers back. American journalist Heidi Levine of the Washington Post was injured in the attack. She described how dozens of settlers ambushed her as she was reporting at the scene. "I got jumped," she said. "I was on the ground and they were kicking me and I was trying to hold onto my camera and my bag. I had my helmet and flak jacket on which protected me. They made me stand up and they kicked me again, and this went on for at least 10 minutes." In a statement, Washington Post executive editor Matt Murray said Levine had been clearly identifiable as a journalist. "We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities," he said. The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said personnel had been despatched to the area "following a report of a violent confrontation". It said a female journalist had been injured during the confrontation. And that "all circumstances" surrounding the incident would be examined. As the farmers retreated, the sound of live ammunition cracked across the fields. It was unclear if settlers or Israeli forces were firing. Minutes later, Israeli forces began firing tear gas into the Palestinian fields to end the confrontation – a well-worn Israeli pattern of managing these conflicts. The UN says settler attacks on the olive harvest this year have so far killed one Palestinian and injured more than 120 others across the West Bank. Illegal Jewish outposts have mushroomed here over the past few years, clustering in closer around Palestinian olive groves. What we witnessed was part of a pattern being repeated day after day, as settler outposts here increase. The yearly olive harvest has become a litmus test of how the policies of Israel's fiercely pro-settlement government are affecting Palestinians here, by presiding over growing violence by extremist settlers, and fuelling Jewish claims to the land. BBC Verify has identified 254 incidents from the past three years the Israeli military said it is reviewing after being accused of harm. Gary Toombs works with international charity Humanity & Inclusion, locating and disposing hazards. Israel said in September it would act in response to UK sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank. The consulate, first established in 1838, was set to be closed by the Israeli government in retaliation for UK sanctions. Many Palestinians are still living in cramped tent cities, with the US plan to end the war largely stalled. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Canada PM warns 'stakes are high' as Alberta separation vote nears
content: Prime Minister Mark Carney has urged Albertans to vote to remain in Canada ahead of an independence referendum, warning that the "stakes are high". Speaking at a pro-unity rally on Thursday in Calgary, Carney said the referendum is taking place "at the worst possible time" and called on voters to deliver a "decisive result" against separation. More than 450,000 Albertans have already voted early or by mail on a question asking if they wish the province to remain part of Canada, or start the process of holding a binding referendum to separate. Campaigners on both sides are making their final pitches ahead of Monday's vote, though polls indicate most Albertans are supportive of a united Canada. Still, Carney said Albertans should not assume that the result is decided based on the polling alone. "Turnout will determine the outcome," he told a crowd of more than 7,000 in Calgary. He also nodded at external pressures facing Canada as a reason to dismiss separation. "The world has become more dangerous and divided. Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us," Carney said, echoing warnings he has made in the past about the threat US tariffs pose to Canada's economy and security. Thursday's rally is one of two back-to-back pro-unity events that the prime minister is scheduled to attend in Alberta, with another one set for tomorrow in Edmonton, his hometown. Earlier in the day, Carney toured several businesses in Calgary and spoke to pro-unity volunteers in a get-out-the-vote push. The 19 October referendum was called by the province's premier Danielle Smith earlier this year after a grassroots group gathered around 300,000 petition signatures asking for a binding referendum on separation. Smith, a Conservative whose political base includes supporters of independence, has advocated for Alberta to remain in Canada but has said the referendum is a chance to hear directly from Albertans on the issue. Supporters of separation say the oil-rich, landlocked province has been overlooked by federal politicians in Ottawa despite the wealth it contributes to Canada. Successive Liberal governments of the last 10 years, they argue, have put environmental policies above helping Alberta develop its oil and gas sector, and that Alberta would get to keep more of its wealth if it splits from Canada. Those who oppose separation say a newly independent Alberta would be left responsible for billions of dollars in debt, and warn that the uncertainty would drive thousands of jobs and investment out of the province. Some, including Prime Minister Carney, have likened the Alberta referendum to "Brexit" when the UK voted to leave the European Union in 2016, warning that a vote to leave may come with unintended economic consequences. In his speech on Thursday, Carney acknowledged that "the frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real". But he said that his government is willing to support Alberta and its energy industry. In the weeks leading up to the referendum, Carney announced his plans to fast-track approval of a new oil pipeline from Alberta to Canada's Pacific coast. He has described the project as "a demonstration of the power of Canada" and argued it would help the country diversify its markets as it deals with US tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump. Along with the ballot on separation, Albertans will also vote on nine other questions - a number focused on whether the province should have more control over its immigration system. Carney urged supporters to "vote no to the nine", signalling a break from Premier Smith, who put the questions on the ballot and who has called on Albertans to support them. In a response on X on Thursday, Smith said she and Carney "have found common ground on many things", but accused him of failing to understand how Liberal immigration policies have affected the cost of living in Alberta. Smith is set to speak at a separate pro-unity event in Calgary on Friday alongside Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre, who has also advocated for Alberta to remain in Canada. Meanwhile, advocates for Alberta separation are planning a rally in Edmonton on Saturday in their own last-minute push to turn out voters. Early figures suggest a strong voter turn-out, with the average number of ballots cast already higher than in Alberta's last provincial general election. Albertans vote this month on staying in Canada or moving ahead to a binding independence referendum. The Parti Québécois, which secured a minority, has vowed to hold an independence referendum in the years to come. Prime Minister Mark Carney has said the military is running scenarios in the unlikely case the US invades Canada. A west coast pipeline project is the first to be fast-tracked and will be a major test of Carney's promise to global investors. It is the latest escalation in the Canada-US trade war after negotiations collapsed in late August, with no word on when talks may resume. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Porn showing choking or incest to be banned from early November, government says
content: Online pornography depicting strangulation or incestuous relationships will be banned from early November, the government has announced. From 6 November, it will be illegal to possess or publish porn which shows strangulation or suffocation, depicts sexual activity between people who are related or shows adults role-playing as children under 16 in England and Wales. The new rules follow a review into porn regulation in 2025 which found depictions of choking were "rife" on popular porn sites and had helped normalise the act among young people. Conservative peer Baroness Gabby Bertin, who headed the review, said the news came "not a moment too soon". She told the Press Association the change in law would "send the unequivocal signal" to companies that host and facilitate porn, and also to wider society, that "extreme and violent content that encourages real-life harm is not acceptable". Her independent review, commissioned by former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak's government, cited an account of a 14-year-old boy asking a teacher how to choke girls during sex . It warned that people imitating such behaviour "may face devastating consequences". Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday, Baroness Bertin said porn showing strangulation had "absolutely sort of normalised this kind of sexual violence". "That has to come to an end and I hope this law change will be the beginning of that," she said - adding that it aimed to "marry up" differences in the law about what was acceptable online and offline. Non-fatal strangulation is already an offence if someone does not consent, but its depiction online is currently not illegal. Amendments to the Crime and Policing Bill, which became law in April, sought to ensure such content would be captured by the legislation and made criminal offences in England and Wales. Justice minister Alex Davies-Jones said it was not about "criminalising harmless sexual preferences". But she said "porn can shape what people think a healthy relationship looks like, especially young people". Content which "normalises, or even glorifies" violence against women can "blur the line with what is acceptable in real life", she said. "If you've got this material, delete it. If you're sharing it, stop," Davies-Jones added. "It's not as harmless as you may think, and after 6 November, it is criminal." The new offences each carry a maximum penalty of five years' imprisonment, for publication. According to the government, this could include uploading, posting or otherwise making the content available to someone online. Possession, meanwhile, could include keeping an image stored on a phone, computer or in cloud storage, the government says. Someone found to be in possession of images depicting sexual activity involving a person pretending to be under 16 could face up to three years' imprisonment, after 6 November. Those found to be in possession of images depicting strangulation, suffocation or penetrative sexual activity between certain relatives could face up to two years' imprisonment. Porn that shows or depicts sex between step or foster-relations where one person is pretending to be under 18 will also be captured by the new offences. Durham University law professor Clare McGlynn - who has previously warned widely available extreme content normalises sexual violence - welcomed the laws taking full effect. "This is a potential turning point, the commencement of these laws marking a line in the sand when we decided that we were no longer going to accept the normalisation of sexually violent content in pornography," she told the BBC. But she said questions remained over how swiftly tech platforms and regulators would act to remove and mitigate the spread of violating material. "While these are criminal offences, this is not about prosecuting individuals, but transforming the online pornographic landscape and that requires the platforms and regulator to act," Prof McGlynn added.
